cards.title: What AI actually is
cards.short: AI is software that finds patterns in data and uses them to answer, predict or create.
facts: It does not 'think' like a person — it calculates probabilities.
It learns from examples, not from rules typed by hand.
The same model can be good at one task and bad at another.
cards.example: When ChatGPT writes a reply, it is predicting the most likely next words, not looking up an answer.

cards.title: How to write a better prompt
cards.short: A good prompt says who, what, how and in what style — in that order.
facts: Be specific: 'a red fox in snow, soft morning light' beats 'an animal'.
Mention the format you want: photo, illustration, 3D, sketch.
Ask for one change at a time when refining a result.
cards.example: 'Cinematic landscape, mountains and a lake at sunrise, 4k, ultra realistic' gives far better output than 'nice scenery'.

cards.title: Passwords that actually protect you
cards.short: Length beats cleverness. A long random password is far safer than a short tricky one.
facts: Use at least 12 characters with mixed types.
Never reuse the same password on two sites.
Turn on two-factor authentication wherever it is offered.
cards.example: 'v7#Kq2!mL9@x' is far harder to crack than 'Rahul@2010', which follows a common pattern.

cards.title: How plants make their own food
cards.short: Plants use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make sugar, releasing oxygen.
facts: The green pigment chlorophyll captures sunlight.
Water is drawn up from the roots by the stem.
Almost every food chain on Earth starts here.
cards.example: A leaf left in sunlight produces tiny oxygen bubbles in water — you can see photosynthesis happen.

cards.title: Why blood groups matter
cards.short: Blood groups are markers on red blood cells; matching them prevents dangerous reactions.
facts: O negative is the universal donor.
AB positive is the universal recipient.
Rh factor (positive or negative) matters as much as A, B and O.
cards.example: In an emergency, O negative blood can be given before a patient's group is known.

cards.title: A light year is distance, not time
cards.short: It is how far light travels in one year — about 9.46 trillion kilometres.
facts: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach us.
The nearest star after the Sun is about 4.2 light years away.
Looking at distant stars means looking into the past.
cards.example: If a star is 100 light years away, the light you see tonight left it 100 years ago.

cards.title: Why Chandrayaan-3 mattered
cards.short: In August 2023 India landed near the Moon's south pole, a region no other mission had reached.
facts: The lander was named Vikram and the rover Pragyan.
The south pole may hold water ice in shadowed craters.
ISRO is India's national space agency.
cards.example: The mission's low-cost engineering became a widely studied model for space programmes.

cards.title: The Constitution in one minute
cards.short: India's Constitution is the rulebook that limits government power and guarantees rights.
facts: It came into effect on 26 January 1950.
Article 14 guarantees equality before the law.
It is the longest written constitution of any country.
cards.example: If a law treats two citizens unequally without good reason, Article 14 can be used to challenge it.

cards.title: India's rivers at a glance
cards.short: Himalayan rivers are perennial; peninsular rivers depend on rainfall.
facts: The Ganga is the longest river within India.
The Godavari is the longest peninsular river.
Himalayan rivers carry glacier melt all year.
cards.example: Because of glacier melt, the Ganga keeps flowing in summer while rain-fed rivers shrink.

cards.title: Learn words from context, not lists
cards.short: A word sticks when you meet it inside a sentence, not alone in a list.
facts: Note the sentence, not just the meaning.
Use a new word within 24 hours of learning it.
Learn word families: decide, decision, decisive.
cards.example: Seeing 'reluctant' in 'he was reluctant to answer' teaches both meaning and usage.

cards.title: The three tenses you actually need
cards.short: Most everyday sentences use present simple, past simple and present perfect.
facts: Present simple: habits and facts — 'she goes'.
Past simple: finished actions — 'she went'.
Present perfect: past linked to now — 'she has gone'.
cards.example: 'I lost my keys' (finished) versus 'I have lost my keys' (still missing).

cards.title: How to solve number series
cards.short: Check differences first, then ratios, then squares and cubes.
facts: Subtract consecutive numbers to see the gap pattern.
If gaps double, the series is multiplying.
Recognise 1, 4, 9, 16 as squares and 1, 8, 27 as cubes.
cards.example: In 2, 6, 12, 20, 30 the gaps are 4, 6, 8, 10 — so the next gap is 12.
